version: arXiv:1611.08832v2; revised March 2017; published in IPCO 2017; PDF 13 pages

topic_relevance.basis: The paper specifies a sequential, independently checkable proof format for LP/IP optimality and infeasibility certificates, with exact-rational arithmetic, integer rounding, branching assumptions, and assumption discharge.

definitions: A linear-inference step derives a valid inequality by taking a combination of the original or previously derived inequalities, with multiplier signs chosen consistently with each inequality direction.

For integer variables, if an inferred inequality has integer coefficients on the integer coordinates, its right-hand side may be rounded up to the next integer; this is the Chvátal–Gomory rounding step.

A split disjunction a^T x<=delta or a^T x>=delta+1, with integer delta and integral a^T x on feasible integer points, is represented by introducing both sides as assumptions, deriving consequences in each branch, then unsplitting to discharge the assumptions.
A certificate is a sequential list of statements whose justification is checked by a small set of inference rules, rather than a replay of the full solver algorithm.

assumptions: Every linear combination is checked with exact rational arithmetic and sign restrictions.
For integer-rounding inferences, coefficients on rounded integer coordinates are integral and the original integer restrictions apply.
theorem_cards.statement: An LP optimum can be certified by deriving the claimed objective lower/upper bound from the constraints through linear inequality inference. A pure-integer bound can additionally use Chvátal–Gomory rounding. For branch-and-cut proofs, a sequential certificate with explicit branch assumptions and unsplitting can certify the final bound or infeasibility.
proof_steps: For an LP, combine constraints with dual-feasible multiplier signs to infer the objective bound; matching a feasible primal objective certifies optimality, while a contradiction certifies infeasibility.

For integer programs, add a rounding rule: from c^T x>=v with integer c on integer coordinates infer c^T x>=ceil(v). The example derives y>=-1/2, rounds to y>=0, then derives x+y>=1/4 and rounds to the integer bound x+y>=1.

For branch-and-cut, introduce the disjuncts as assumptions; each local derivation carries the assumptions it depends on. At sibling leaves, unsplitting discharges the corresponding disjunction, working bottom-up until no branch assumption remains.

The paper renders a small infeasible two-variable integer system as a ten-line sequential proof; its PDF table was visually checked to recover OCR-damaged fractional coefficients in the derivation rows.
gaps: The complete formal syntax and all inference rules are specified in the accompanying VIPR files, not reproduced in full in this article.
The article restricts its operational description to a branch-and-cut regime with split cuts and does not claim that every possible MIP solver operation already has a rule in the format.

assumptions: The certificate contains a final claim derived from listed input constraints and prior derivations.
The checker uses exact rational arithmetic and validates every reason locally.
theorem_cards.statement: The independent checker need not reproduce the optimization search: it validates the listed derivations sequentially. A preprocessing pass can remove unused statements and topologically reorder dependencies; the reported experiments found checking faster than solving on the tested instances.
proof_steps: Generate a proof trace during search; form its derivation-dependency graph; retain the component ending at the final claim; topologically reorder it; then check each rational inference and assumption discharge.
gaps: Runtime ratios are empirical for the paper's tested SCIP instances and hardware, not a worst-case complexity theorem.

The original solver and certificate checker can still share modeling errors; the certificate checks entailment from the encoded model, not whether that model correctly represents the intended mathematics.

constant_dependence: No numerical inequality constant is established. Certificate size can be large and depends on the proof/search trace; the paper reports computational results for 107 MIP instances and shows that a tightening pass can remove substantial redundancy. Exactness depends on rational input and rational checking, not floating-point tolerances.
endpoint_limits: A checked certificate proves a claim about the encoded rational model; it does not certify that the model faithfully encodes the external problem.
The article explicitly notes that short polynomial-size certificates for general MIP optimality/infeasibility may not exist.
LP dual certificates are simpler; integer rounding and split assumptions are needed for the discrete problem.
Floating-point solver statuses, matching solver outputs, or a feasible point alone do not certify global MIP optimality.
Certificate validity is only as complete as the supported inference rules; arbitrary solver presolve or cuts must be represented by checked derivations or justified separately.
reusable_methods: Write the claimed result as a final statement and require each step to cite a short, checkable inference rule.
Separate search from verification: allow a complicated optimizer to discover the proof while keeping the verifier small and independent.
Use exact rational arithmetic for the certificate checker; when using interval arithmetic instead, require outward-rounded enclosure rules and check their soundness separately.
Treat branching as assumptions and explicitly discharge each assumption by an exhaustive disjunction, rather than trusting a search tree summary.
Keep a model-validation check outside the proof checker so an internally valid certificate is not mistaken for correctness of the original encoding.
unchecked: The precise VIPR file-format specification and C++ checker source are cited but were not in the paper corpus and were not inspected.
The example certificates and fractions on PDF pages 6 and 8 were rendered and visually checked; no other formula required visual correction.
The proof system's soundness argument is presented through inference-rule semantics and examples, not as a single separately labeled meta-theorem with a full formalization in the article.
